sweep_summary: Five title hits, all Glottolog. Two are one dissertation (Al-Mozainy 1981, UT Austin), the classic primary Bedouin (Harb) Hijazi source: no open copy exists (UT repository and HathiTrust blocked to download, archive.org/CORE empty), priority high for acquisition; its rule survives second-hand in Oh 1998 (held by the project from the earlier reading) and now in Hagberg 1993 (downloaded from archive.org, UMI edition of the 2006 SIL e-book Glottolog lists), pp.74-75 ex.(29)-(30): final superheavy > heavy penult > antepenult, which confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding. Kabrah 2014 (Makkan, Benjamins, paywalled): abstract confirms a 3-syllable window with heavy syllables attracting stress, end rule right, and adds a lexically stressed /-at/ suffix and post-lexical opacity — medium priority as a possible refinement. Alahmari 2020 (Benjamins, paywalled) is about a Southwestern Saudi dialect with pre-antepenultimate stress, a different variety that Glottolog lumps under hija1235; silent on the catalog's Urban/Bedouin Hijazi record, low priority with a scope flag. Nothing read supersedes Al Solami 2022 / Al-Mohanna 2004.org and repository APIs.

new_statements.quote: (29) Stress in Bedouin Hijazi Arabic (Al-Mozainy 1981): (a) Stress is on the last syllable if it is superheavy (CVVC or CVCC). (b) Otherwise, stress is on the penult if it is heavy (CVV or CVC). (c) Otherwise, stress is on the antepenult. Each of the three cases described in (29) is illustrated in (30): The final syllable is superheavy in (a) but not in (b) or (c), which correspond to (29) (b) and (c), respectively. (30) (a) maktuub 'written', darabt 'I hit' (b) maktuufah 'tied (f.sg.)', gaabilna 'meet us (m.sg.)' (c) maalana 'our property', yasribin 'they (f.) drink'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement, which was itself extracted from the 1993 edition of this work; so this is a confirmation of the record, not an independent source. It refines the catalog's empty rule field with the weight rule, the ordering of stress before Low Vowel Deletion, and the surface exceptions. Second-hand for Al-Mozainy 1981.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weight-driven stress in a right-edge three-syllable window: stress the final syllable if it is superheavy (CVVC or CVCC); otherwise stress the penult if it is heavy (CVV or CVC); otherwise stress the antepenult. Hagberg restates Al-Mozainy 1981 via Al-Mozainy, Bley-Vroman & McCarthy 1985 (not first-hand), and uses the language to show that stress survives deletion of its host vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated: Hagberg states (p.74) that the study concerns only the derivation of primary stress, not distinctive degrees of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Surface exceptions created by Low Vowel Deletion (a -> 0 / C__[Ca]a, ex. (31)): forms such as ?inksarat 'she got broken' and ?ixtbaraw 'they took an exam' (ex. (33)) violate (29) on the surface because stress is assigned before deletion and the stress of the deleted vowel shifts to the following vowel (stability). Hagberg compares Tiberian Hebrew, Negev Bedouin Arabic and Unami.
new_statements.identity_note: Hagberg's data are Bedouin Hijazi Arabic (Al-Mozainy 1981's dialect). Al-Mohanna 2021 describes Urban Hijazi Arabic (UHA), which he groups with the 'differential dialects' of Arabic (high vowels delete in unstressed non-final open syllables, low vowels do not). Both fall under Glottolog hija1235 (Hijazi Arabic); the catalog record is named simply 'Arabic'. The catalog's weight coding rests on the Bedouin variety only.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were found verbatim in the text files we hold at the stated locators (Al Solami 2022 sec.3-4, pp.3-6; Al-Mohanna 2004 ex.(18) p.7, table (20) p.8, fn.11 p.18). The classification 'weight' (final superheavy > heavy penult > heavy antepenult, final CV/CVC light, right-edge three-syllable window, no secondary stress) is exactly what both sources state, and is independently matched by the held Omar 1975 FSI course rules and by Oh 1998's restatement of Al-Mozainy 1981 (downloaded now, KU open access, scanned). The StressTyp2 'U-P/A' code encodes the same rule, so the flagged partial mismatch is notational. Better-in-principle sources are unpublished dissertations (Al-Mozainy 1981, Al-Mohanna 1998, Jarrah 1993, Kabrah 2004) that all secondary reports show agreeing with the classification

sources.quote: 'In BHA, stress falls on one of the last three syllables. Stress falls on the final syllable if it is superheavy (CV:C or CVCC) ... maktu:b, darabt. If the final syllable is not superheavy and the penultimate is heavy (CV: or CVC), the penultimate receives stress ... maktu:fah, ga:bilna. If the final syllable is not superheavy and the penultimate is not heavy, stress falls on the antepenultimate ... ma:lana, yashribin. sources.citation: Alzaidi, Muhammad Swaileh A. 2022. Pitch Accent Distribution and Focus Structure in Taifi Arabic: A Production Study. International Journal of English Linguistics 12(1): 179-196 (published online 22 December 2021). doi:10.5539/ijel.v12n1p179
sources.note: Classifies Taifi/Hijazi Arabic with Arabic dialects generally as a stress-accent language: stress is lexical (higher F0, longer duration, stronger intensity on the stressed syllable) and pitch accents are intonational, phonologically associated with the lexically stressed syllable; every content word bears an (L+)H* pitch accent, post-focus deaccenting rare (23%). No lexical tone; F0 is post-lexical. Gives the urban Hijazi word-stress algorithm with examples (Table 1).

tone.quote: Arabic dialects in general are stress-accent language (McCarthy, 1979; Watson, 2002). Stress is used at the lexical level in which one of the syllables is realized with higher F0, longer duration and stronger intensity (...). In addition, intonational pitch accent phonologically associate with the lexically stressed syllable (Hellmuth, 2006; Alzaidi et al., 2019). Stress assignment is predictable in Arabic. It is determined based on (1) syllable weight and (2) syllable position in the lexical word. In ‘urban’ Hijazi Arabic, stress falls on a final syllable if it is superheavy (CVVC or CVCC), else on a heavy penultimate (CVV or CVC) (Abaalkhail, 1998).
tone.locator: p.181, sec. 2.2 'Taifi Arabic', with Table 1 'Word-level stress assignment in urban Hijazi Arabic'

sources.note: First systematic acoustic study of focus prosody in HA; treats all F0 events as intonational pitch accents whose docking sites are the lexically stressed syllables ('The F0 peak is placed within the lexically stressed syllable in every word'), on-focus pitch-range expansion and post-focus compression (+PFC). No claim of lexical tone; lexical tone is mentioned only for Mandarin comparisons. Restates the urban HA stress algorithm from Al-Mohanna 1998:222 incl. clause (d) even-syllable-count default.

tone.quote: the lexically–stressed syllables in Arabic, including Egyptian Arabic, and of HA in particular (as it will be shown later in this study), are said to be the docking sites of pitch accents (Hellmuth, 2006). Therefore, the first task in our intonational analysis is to determine where lexical stress occurs. (8) a. Stress a final superheavy syllable (CVVC or CVCC). b. Otherwise, stress a heavy penult (CVV or CVC). c. Otherwise, stress a heavy antepenult. d. Otherwise, stress the [light] penult or the antepenult, whichever is separated from the first preceding heavy syllable or (if there is none) from the beginning of the word by an even number of syllables. (Al-Mohanna, 1998, p. 222)

sources.note: Under focus the stressed syllable of the focused Makkan Arabic word gets a wider F0 excursion, higher F0 and stronger intensity, but the words after the focus are not compressed, unlike Egyptian, Hijazi and Lebanese Arabic. The abstract presupposes lexical word stress and adds its acoustic correlates under focus; it says nothing about where stress falls, so the catalog's weight-based rule is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

tone.says: Focus prosody of Makkan Arabic - the on-focus word expands excursion size, raises F0 and intensity of its stressed syllable; information vs contrastive focus not prosodically distinct; Makkan lacks post-focus compression (unlike Hijazi/Taifi, Egyptian, Lebanese); focus recognition low. Intonation/F0 study of a stress-accent dialect; nothing on lexical tone expected.

Heavy syllables attract stress, with end rule right. Makkan also exhibits some cases of opaque stress, where stress appears in unexpected positions. Opacity of stress is evident at the phrasal level after.. syncope and initial epenthesis. Morphologically conditioned stress is also evident in Makkan where the feminine subject marker /-at/ "she" is lexically stressed.' Abstract-level: weight-driven, right-edge three-syllable window = the catalog's 'we…
